articles.title: Spanberger voting-rights letters sent to dead felons amid ballot access push
articles.summary: Deceased Virginians with felony convictions are reportedly receiving voting-rights restoration letters signed by Gov. Abigail Spanberger's office.
articles.body: Deceased Virginians with felony convictions are reportedly among those receiving voting-rights restoration letters under Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who announced in July that she had restored voting rights to 66,000 people with felony convictions. The notices come as Virginia separately implements a federal court ruling that sharply narrowed which felony convictions can trigger disenfranchisement, while voters this fall will decide whether to amend the state constitution to automatically restore voting rights upon release from incarceration. "I've been a lawyer for 27 years and in every minute of my career, when you were convicted of a felony, you lose your voting rights. The way you get those back is you have to petition the governor and then the governor can review your case and determine whether the civil rights of a convicted felon should be restored," Virginia Beach attorney Tim Anderson told Fox News Digital on Monday. Anderson, who shared posts showing letters from Spanberger and her administration sent to families of deceased recipients, said the situation is "one or the other" — either Richmond is not vetting who receives the restoration notifications or its vetting is not thorough enough to catch deceased recipients. SPANBERGER SPARKS OUTRAGE AFTER SNEAKILY ENDING YOUNGKIN-ERA WOMEN'S SPORTS PROTECTIONS "The order specifically says that they've reviewed [each] case individually, right?" He noted that Virginia has online voter registration and questioned whether an unscrupulous relative who received one of the notifications might try to register their dead relative to vote. "These dead people clearly aren't petitioning the governor to get their civil liberties back... they're restoring every single felon's civil disabilities without anybody even asking. And that's concerning, especially when they're dead." Virginia resident Howard "Skip" Lambert posted a July 1 restoration notice signed by Spanberger and an Aug. 31 notification from her administration addressed to a redacted relative, informing the recipient that their voting rights had been restored. The July letter said that after the relative had been convicted and sentenced, Spanberger’s office "completed review of the particulars of the individual’s case." Anderson pointed to that line as evidence of vetting. Lambert’s letter went on to say the relative would have their civil rights — except for the ability to transport or possess firearms — restored effective July 1. VIRGINIA GOVERNOR ABIGAIL SPANBERGER QUIETLY ROLLS BACK YOUNGKIN'S PLANS TO PROTECT GIRLS' SPORTS In the ensuing letter from Secretary of the Commonwealth Candi Mundon-King, the relative was notified that Spanberger had restored their right to vote and serve on a jury and was encouraged to re-register to vote at the online "Citizen’s Portal" via a QR code. Lambert wrote that he was upset by the mailings, saying the recipient was his daughter, who died in 2024. He also confirmed that she had a felony conviction. "Interesting this letter arrives as early-voting begins... yet the provided official order is dated July 1," he said on Sept. 24. "Just because cash doesn't change hands doesn't mean the governor isn't trying to buy votes. Reached by phone Monday, the Fredericksburg-area resident confirmed to Fox News Digital that the documents were authentic and that the recipient was his daughter. "I do have a question of timing in the letter I believe my daughter voted in the previous election where it was Hillary and Donald Trump — because she had had her rights restored then," he said. Around the time of that election, former Democratic Gov. Terence McAuliffe attempted a mass restoration but was rebuked by the Virginia Supreme Court, which ruled that he did not have the authority to take such an action affecting an estimated 206,000 Virginians, according to NPR. Another woman, Peggie Young, posted a similar set of documents addressed to her "dear BFF, Peter Breton." "I have his ashes. Is this perhaps how voter fraud begins. I'm so confused," she said, adding that she also received the letter only on Sept. 29. Young could not immediately be reached. Virginia House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Gate City, told Fox News Digital that Spanberger's purported vetting process appears to be inadequate: "If the process is so thorough that they can't even tell who's alive and who's dead, how thorough is it?" Kilgore told Fox News Digital. The federal case began in 2023 as King v. Youngkin, when disenfranchised Virginians sued then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin and other state officials, arguing that Virginia’s blanket felony ban conflicted with the federal Virginia Readmission Act of 1870. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER U.S. District Judge John Gibney Jr. ruled in January that Virginia could disenfranchise people only for 11 common-law felonies recognized in 1870. After rejecting the state’s effort to map those offenses onto a broader list of modern crimes, Virginia ultimately narrowed automatic disenfranchisement to murder, voluntary manslaughter and involuntary manslaughter. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Department of Elections is separately notifying roughly 235,000 Virginians whose convictions no longer disqualify them from voting. Those court-driven notices are distinct from the Spanberger restoration orders received by Lambert and Young, which state that the governor’s office reviewed each recipient’s case before restoring multiple civil rights. Fox News Digital reached out to Spanberger's office and ELECT for comment.

articles.title: Biden's 'anti-MAGA task force' sparked internal alarm across DOJ, new report shows
articles.summary: Merrick Garland's school board memo triggered internal revolt at the Department of Justice, with one official dubbing it the "Anti-MAGA Task Force."
articles.body: The Biden administration’s effort to combat alleged threats against school boards amid a wave of heated parent protests triggered sustained internal resistance within the Justice Department and FBI, documents released by the DOJ show. "Five years ago, Attorney General Merrick Garland issued an infamous memorandum at the urging of the National School Boards Association and White House officials, directing the FBI and United States Attorneys to consider looking for a federal hook to prosecute parents exercising their right to free speech," Blanche posted to X on Monday, when the DOJ released the "Report to Expose the Weaponization of Government Against Parents in Schools." "Along with the report, we’ve released hundreds of exhibits and emails that make official and verify what many Americans had guessed: the Garland DOJ worked hand in hand with WH officials and the National School Boards Association to chill free speech and parental rights while they threatened to prosecute parents and label them domestic terrorists," Blanche added. In October 2021, Attorney General Merrick Garland issued a memo directing the FBI and U.S. Attorneys to coordinate with federal, state and local law enforcement over what it described as an "increase in harassment, intimidation and threats of violence against school board members, teachers and workers in our nation’s public schools," amid escalating clashes involving parents at school board meetings. TRUMP DOJ REPORT LAYS BARE BIDEN ADMINISTRATION'S ALLEGED ANTI-CHRISTIAN BIAS Garland’s memo drew significant internal pushback across the Justice Department and FBI, with officials raising concerns about politicization, First Amendment protections and whether there was a sufficient federal basis for intervention, according to the Justice Department report released Monday. The memo followed throngs of parents protesting at school board meetings over dissatisfaction with how gender and race were being taught in classrooms and COVID-19-era learning restrictions, prompting the National School Boards Association (NSBA) to appeal to then-President Joe Biden for federal assistance and warn that some actions surrounding the protests "could be equivalent to a form of domestic terrorism and hate crimes." Some of the internal messages detailed in the Justice Department’s report released Monday had been disclosed previously and reported on by Fox News Digital. In one message sent before Garland’s memo went public on Oct. 4, 2021, a deputy assistant attorney general said the operation — and proposals to link it to the DOJ’s election crimes work — looked so politically motivated that Garland "might as well rename the damn thing the Anti-MAGA Task Force." The DOJ’s Public Integrity Section chief, meanwhile, called the proposal "stupid." An FBI counterterrorism official later raised concerns about the label "domestic terrorist" potentially being applied to everyone who "oppose school board actions," while a DOJ Civil Rights Division attorney noted that much of the activity in question could be protected under the parents’ First Amendment rights. DOJ LAWSUIT TARGETS ALLEGED SCHOOL ‘SECRET GENDER TRANSITIONS’ POLICIES THAT KEEP PARENTS IN THE DARK Multiple DOJ officials noted that the problem at hand appeared to fall primarily within the jurisdiction of state and local authorities and questioned whether there was a sufficient federal basis to intervene, according to the report. Internal dissent over the effort continued as the memo was implemented following its Oct. 4, 2021, release and during the resulting fallout. On Oct. 5, 2021, an FBI lawyer claimed that the DOJ issued the press release accompanying the memo without coordinating with the bureau. The Deputy Assistant Director of the FBI’s Criminal Investigative Division, the agency’s largest operational division, stated that "we were all caught off guard by this announcement," which was "unilaterally pushed by DOJ." As the DOJ began assembling its task force, objections persisted. BLISTERING REPORT EXPOSES HOW NATIONAL K-12 GROUP'S DEI AGENDA IS TRICKLING DOWN TO LOCAL SCHOOLS The Deputy Assistant Attorney General in the DOJ's National Security Division stated that he didn’t "see the need for a task force like this" and that the Justice Department doesn’t "start a narrowly focused task force every time some group believes they are the subject of threat." Later that month, the Department of Homeland Security circulated a brief linking the threat level facing educational workers as tied to heightened opposition to masks, vaccines and critical race theory. An FBI counterterrorism official slammed the threat assessment guidelines as a "politically charged paper," expressing his desire that the FBI not collaborate. NSBA ultimately apologized for the language used in its letter to then-President Joe Biden seeking federal assistance, including action by the Justice Department and FBI. "The obligation of the Justice Department is to protect the American people against violence and threats of violence and that particularly includes public officials," he said of the memo. Some school board officials did receive online and written threats in 2021, a fact supporters of Garland’s approach cited in defending the Justice Department’s response. articles.title: Emerging tech has new Army leaders warning troops can't ‘AI’ their way to victory on the battlefield
articles.summary: Gen. Christopher LaNeve says command and control is the Army's top modernization priority as new leadership narrows its sweeping transformation push.
articles.body: Amid a rapid rise in technological developments, the U.S. Army’s new leadership is looking to pull back on using artificial intelligence and other tools it feels forced the branch to transform too much all at once. Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army vice chief serving as acting chief of staff, outlined on Monday how he hopes to narrow the service’s sweeping modernization push after years of experimentation with drones, artificial intelligence and other emerging technology. "There was a lot, a lot of motion," LaNeve told a small group of reporters. "It was almost like everything was being transformed at once." "You can't AI yourself to be the best maneuver brigade commander out there," LaNeve said. The Army Transformation Initiative pushed new technology rapidly into formations and encouraged experimentation across the board. Army leaders credited that effort with accelerating change but acknowledged Monday that its breadth created enormous activity across the force. INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH The branch is now preparing to unveil "How the Army Fights," a new framework intended to turn years of experimentation into a more focused set of decisions about what technology the service will prioritize, where it belongs in Army formations and how the force will organize and spend for future wars. "The Army cannot and should not modernize everything at once," the new blueprint states. "The answer is focused modernization." Sgt. Maj. of the Army Michael Weimer said experimentation through the technology push produced necessary learning, but insisted that the service had reached a point where it needed to "drop the chalk line and actually start making some decisions." Those decisions include which technologies warrant investment, where they belong in Army formations and which theaters take priority — with the service acknowledging it cannot afford to transform everything simultaneously. Army leaders aren't yet saying what will fall by the wayside. Asked what was being left "on the cutting room floor" as the service narrows its focus, LaNeve said, "I'm not sure we're prepared to say what we're cutting out now." But one investment is moving unmistakably to the front of the line. "If you ask me what my number one modernization priority would be, I would say command and control," LaNeve said. The shift is unfolding amid a broader leadership shake-up at the Army. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle took over after his predecessor, Dan Driscoll, resigned last month following months of reported friction with War Secretary Pete Hegseth, who had earlier ousted Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, a close Driscoll ally who helped lead the service’s transformation push. Telle, a former Trump White House aide, was tapped days later to lead the Army in an acting capacity and was publicly praised by Hegseth as "strong and whip smart." In his first press interview since taking the job, Telle described "How the Army Fights" as a way to impose greater coherence on the service’s modernization efforts as technology rapidly changes the battlefield. TRUMP NAMES ADAM TELLE ACTING SECRETARY OF THE ARMY FOLLOWING DAN DRISCOLL'S RESIGNATION That battlefield is envisioned as one in which troops operate alongside autonomous systems and under persistent drone surveillance, while AI helps commanders sift through massive amounts of sensor data and identify targets in "seconds and minutes rather than hours." The Army also wants autonomous systems taking on some of the most dangerous jobs that are currently performed by soldiers — this includes reconnaissance, resupply and breaching enemy obstacles. But Army leaders are resisting the idea that advances in drones and AI have diminished the importance of traditional ground forces. "Autonomous systems enable Soldiers to destroy and disrupt, but they can never replace the human judgment, leadership, and physical presence of Soldiers required to control the land and consolidate gains," the blueprint states. The Army is drawing heavily from recent conflicts, including Ukraine, Gaza and the India-Pakistan conflict, while building the new framework around its most demanding potential adversary: China. HTAF identifies China's People's Liberation Army as the "pacing threat" and says the Army must organize, train and equip against it with the same institutional focus Cold War-era leaders brought to the Soviet Union. The blueprint also assumes a future major war could reach much closer to home. It warns the U.S. homeland can no longer be treated as a sanctuary, with adversaries potentially using cyberattacks, sabotage and drones to disrupt the ports, airfields and other infrastructure needed to deploy American forces. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For Telle, the challenge is fitting rapidly evolving technology into a coherent Army rather than chasing every new system that emerges. He compared individual weapons and technologies to ornaments on a Christmas tree. "How the Army Fights is really the tree to hang those ornaments on," Telle said.

articles.title: José Andrés planta cara a Óscar Puente tras llamarle "cuñado": "Menos X y mejor transporte público"
articles.standfirst: El chef responde con dureza al ministro de Transportes después de que este arremetiera contra sus críticas a las medidas del Gobierno sobre la vivienda
articles.summary: El chef responde con dureza al ministro de Transportes después de que este arremetiera contra sus críticas a las medidas del Gobierno sobre la vivienda
articles.body: El enfrentamiento entre José Andrés y Óscar Puente ha subido de tono en X. El cocinero y fundador de World Central Kitchen ha respondido al ministro de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible después de que este le calificara de "cuñado" por sus críticas a las medidas del Gobierno para afrontar el problema de la vivienda. El origen de la polémica está en unas declaraciones de José Andrés a El Mundo. El chef defendió que el principal problema de la vivienda en España es la falta de oferta y cuestionó las medidas aprobadas hasta ahora. "España no tiene un problema de falta de decretos. Tiene un problema de falta de viviendas", aseguró. José Andrés criticó que subvencionar la demanda sin aumentar la oferta puede presionar los precios y defendió un incremento de la construcción como vía para afrontar la escasez. Su propuesta la resumió en tres ideas: "Más oferta. Más construcción. Más casas". Las palabras del cocinero provocaron la reacción de Óscar Puente, que respondió en X con duras críticas y lo calificó de "cuñado", además de acusarle de haber protagonizado un "ridículo histórico". Lejos de pasar por alto el comentario, José Andrés ha decidido contestar al ministro y llevar la discusión al terreno de las competencias de Transportes. "Sr. Ministro, dedíquese a conseguir que los transportes públicos funcionen", ha escrito. El chef ha puesto como ejemplo su experiencia en Ucrania, donde, según ha relatado, ha visto funcionar los trenes con puntualidad pese a encontrarse el país en plena guerra. También ha denunciado los problemas de las conexiones ferroviarias en el Campo de Gibraltar y ha cuestionado el estado de las carreteras españolas. José Andrés ha restado importancia al calificativo utilizado por Óscar Puente, pero ha puesto el foco en la responsabilidad institucional del ministro: "Puede llamarme 'cuñado', hacer bromas o faltarme al respeto. Es lo de menos. Lo importante es que usted es el ministro y responde por su gestión". Y José Andrés ha terminado su mensaje con una frase que ha resumido el tono de su respuesta: "Menos X y mejor transporte público. Y si no sabe hacerlo, deje paso a quien pueda. Gracias". El debate sobre la vivienda ha acabado así convertido en un duro intercambio público entre el chef y el ministro de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible, con dos cuestiones distintas en el centro de la polémica: la falta de oferta de vivienda y el funcionamiento del transporte público.

articles.title: Trump rallies in city where alleged MS-13 ‘assassination squad’ leader was busted
articles.summary: President Donald Trump heads to Grand Island, Nebraska, for a rally in the city where an alleged MS-13 hit squad leader was arrested last year.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is heading to Nebraska on Monday to campaign for Republicans in the same city where federal authorities last year captured an alleged MS-13 hit squad leader wanted for four murders in Honduras. Trump will headline a rally in Grand Island alongside U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and Gov. Jim Pillen as part of a multi-state swing ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. articles.title: Liberal haven festival-goers weigh government seizure of their homes: 'I'd be so game'
articles.summary: Takoma Park residents just outside of Washington D.C. were asked whether they'd support government seizure of their own homes and private property during a street festival Sunday.
articles.body: During a Sunday street festival in a notoriously liberal Maryland hotspot just across the Washington, D.C. border, some attendees told Fox News Digital they wouldn't mind if the government seized their property, including their homes. "Yeah, I mean broadly," said Maryland resident Matt Volk when asked if he would support the government taking his home. "It's highly situational, but I definitely think that there's a lot of privately owned land and property that would be better put to use for public use, for resources and housing and things like that for people who are in need of things like that." Fox News Digital took to the streets during a rainy Sunday at the Takoma Park Street Festival to interview area residents about just how much power they would be willing to cede to the government as socialism becomes increasingly popular, especially among younger Americans. Takoma Park is a liberal bastion just outside the nation's capital, where homes and businesses are adorned with LGBT pride paraphernalia, along with decorations marking their support for other leftist causes like the Black Lives Matter movement. YOUNG SWING-STATE VOTERS COZY UP TO DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS, SAY PARTY ESTABLISHMENT MUST ‘LEARN’ FROM DSA WINS One attendee, Karen Irwin, sported a t-shirt that said "Auntifa: Making White men uncomfortable since 1975." She agreed with Volk's sentiment. "I mean, if we were all doing it, I'd be so game," she said. "Do you know what I mean? And who's coming to me? Is this a decision I'm making through democratic means? Then yes, yes, I would be so game. If I voted for it, sure." "You want to be able to keep your property. From what time are we talking? From what in the history of this country? Is it just right now, from right now moving forward, whatever it is you have?" Irwin asked. "Or, you know, 100 years ago, when someone else had it. But the government might have taken it away for whatever reason." A Fox News poll from March found that 38% of those asked said it was a good idea to move away from capitalism and towards socialism. SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' Very liberal voters (66%) and Democrats under age 45 (66%) are those most likely to think moving to socialism would be good. More than half of all Democrats (55%), Black voters (55%) and those under age 30 (53%) also favor moving away from capitalism. While the majority of Americans, especially Republicans and conservatives, still reject socialism, only 51% say capitalism is working well. The other 49% say it isn't. A third person at the Takoma Park street fair on Sunday said the government seizure of his home was a possibility. "I don't know that I would necessarily love it, but I mean, if it was something that was beneficial I'd at least consider it," said Jaw Blake, a Maryland resident. "Nobody wants what they have to be taken away from them, but there is something we said about like you can set up things so that they're available for everybody." THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE. YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM Not everyone interviewed by Fox News Digital was entirely convinced of the idea of government seizure and redistribution of private property. Jenny Sniderman said she doesn't want to give up her property to the government, but that it wasn't out of the question if she was paid to do so. "Of course I don't want to give up my private property," she said. "Are they going to reimburse me fairly? That would be helpful in making my choice." Steve Ney isn't in favor of his home being seized by the government, but he advocated for another socialist policy that recently was implemented in New York City by Mayor Zohran Mamdani. NEW YORK CITY LANDLORDS WARN AMERICAN DREAM IS SLIPPING AWAY UNDER SOCIALIST RENT POLICIES "I think the idea of rent stabilization, for example, is an excellent idea where you limit the rate of increase in rent in order to help people stay in their homes," he said. New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board voted 7-1 in July to halt increases in rent for one and two year leases on rent-stabilized apartments, enacting a core promise from socialist Mamdani's agenda. The policy has faced legal challenges and backlash from property owners in the Big Apple. Real Estate Board of New York (REBNY) President James Whelan blasted Mamdani's effort. "The mayor's report focuses on symptoms, not causes," he told Fox News Digital in August. "New Yorkers are paying record-high rents because there is not enough housing, and many of the reported conditions are concentrated in heavily rent-stabilized buildings that are facing significant operational and financial challenges." MAMDANI RIPPED OVER RECORD-HIGH NYC RENTS WITH CRITICS POINTING TO POLICY THEY SAY IS FUELING CRISIS One Takoma Park Street Festival attendee, Nina Gilden Seavy, a self-identified historian, outrightly rejected the idea that the government should be involved of distributing resources. "I think that's a ridiculous idea. I mean, that's, it's a fool's errand," she said. "The idea that somehow we're gonna be better off if the government is in charge of allocating all resources that sounds not in any way desirable." articles.title: Who is Michele Tafoya? Meet the sideline reporter turned GOP Senate candidate vying to turn Minnesota red
articles.summary: “I’m not gonna stay on the sidelines any longer,” Tafoya said while announcing her bid in one of the country’s most pivotal midterm races.
articles.body:
When it comes to the battle for control of the U.S. Senate, Republicans are mostly playing defense. The lion's share of the races that will decide which party secures a majority in November are in red states — including Texas, Iowa and Ohio — where the GOP is hoping to hold on against ascendant Democratic challengers.

Minnesota is one of the few states in the country where the party is in a position to go on offense and potentially turn a blue seat red.

In pursuit of that goal, the GOP has put its hopes in Michele Tafoya , a former sports broadcaster and NFL sideline reporter turned politician who polls suggest has a real chance of winning in a state that has been dominated by Democrats in recent election cycles.

Tafoya is running for the seat currently held by Democrat Tina Smith, who is not pursuing re-election. Instead her opponent will be Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flannagan , a progressive who supports policies like Medicare for All and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Minnesota has been at the center of some of the biggest controversies of President Trump's second term, particularly his administration's sweeping immigration crackdown. Though a majority of Minnesotans disapprove of Trump's performance as president, Tafoya has steadily chipped away at Flanagan's lead in polls since the primary.

Here's what you need to know about who she is, what she stands for and how she went from the sidelines to the center of one of the midterms' most pivotal races.

Tafoya was born and raised in Southern California. Her father was an aeronautical engineer, and her mother was a school teacher. She has Hispanic heritage on her father's side.

She married her husband, Mark Vandersall, in 2000. They have two children. Tafoya has been open about her struggles with infertility , which included several miscarriages. Her daughter, Oliva, was adopted from Colombia as a nod to her father's lineage.

After launching her sports broadcasting career in Los Angeles, she moved to Minnesota in the early 1990s to take a job at the KFAN sports radio station in Minneapolis. Before long, she moved on to a national role with CBS, which proved to be the jumping-off point for a decades-long career that made her one of the country's most recognizable sports broadcasters. She covered five Super Bowls, the NBA and the Olympics — winning five Emmys for her work along the way.

Tafoya's last broadcast was during Super Bowl LVI in 2022. Her political career began the very next day. Less than 12 hours after the game ended, she announced that she would co-chair the campaign of Republican Kendall Qualls in his bid to become Minnesota governor.

How did she go from NFL sidelines to the campaign trail?

Tafoya has said she always had strong political views, but made a specific effort to keep them out of her work as a broadcaster.

"I was not as free to be as vocal about world events that I'm concerned about," she told The Athletic in 2022. "It's not because I was told to shut up. I want to be very clear about that. But look, if you're on a show like Sunday Night Football … the last thing they want to do is invite controversy."

Tafoya was more open about her beliefs outside on social media, where she would regularly promote work from conservative outlets . But she also made statements that broke from the GOP mainstream, including support for efforts to curb climate change. In an interview with Sports Illustrated in 2015, she described herself as a "pro-choice" conservative with "definite libertarian strains."

After retiring from broadcasting, Tafoya made several appearances as a speaker at Republican political events, including the Conservative Political Action Conference. She was also a guest host on The View , taking on the role of the conservative-leaning voice in contrast to the show's more liberal regular panelists.

In 2022, Tafoya launched a podcast that frequently touched on political topics and featured Republican politicians as guests. The most recent episode , released in January, includes an interview with former My Pillow CEO Mike Lindell, who unsuccessfully ran for Minnesota governor this year despite an endorsement from President Trump.

Tafoya formally announced her Senate bid a few weeks later. In August, she comfortably won a crowded Republican primary to set up a head-to-head race against Flanagan in November.

In her pitch to Minnesota voters, Tafoya has leaned into her sports background.

"I'm not gonna stay on the sidelines any longer," she said while standing on a snow-covered football field in her campaign announcement video.

Like other swing-state Republicans across the country, Tafoya has worked to find a balance between supporting Trump and pushing back on some of his most unpopular policies.

She has supported the president throughout the war with Iran, at one point telling Minnesotans to "take one less trip to Starbucks" to help offset the rising cost of gas. More recently, though, she has joined a growing list of GOP candidates who have called for Trump to end the conflict.

"No president of either party should have a blank check to wage war without the consent of Congress or the buy-in of the American people. That includes President Donald Trump," Tafoya told Twin Cities local news KSTP on Saturday.

Tafoya added that she would be "inclined to vote to end this war" if given the opportunity in the Senate. She has also said she didn't agree with ICE's tactics in Minneapolis and described Trump's tariff policies as "hit or miss."

Her policy views mostly align with mainstream Republican positions. She backs strong immigration enforcement and Trump's mass deportation campaign, a "tough on crime" approach to public safety, tax cuts, and laws barring transgender athletes from competing in women's and girls' sports. On abortion, she says she agrees with the Supreme Court's decision overturning Roe v. Wade , but personally believes there should be "reasonable access" in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

Tafoya's own opinions of Trump have evolved as well. In 2022, she published an open letter urging Trump not to run for a second term, describing his previous time in the White House as "absolute mayhem." She also said on her podcast around the same time that there was much about Trump that she found "difficult to accept."

But during the 2024 presidential campaign, Tafoya said she was supporting Trump with "more enthusiasm" than before. She also said she felt "sort of agnostic" on the Jan. 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol. She celebrated Trump's victory later that year, describing it as "morning in America" — a reference to Ronald Reagan's famous phrase from the 1980s.

Tafoya has mostly left Trump out of her current campaign ads and speeches, instead focusing her messaging on issues like fraud, affordability and public safety. The president opted not to endorse a candidate in Minnesota's Republican primary and has yet to throw his support behind Tafoya in the general election.

Tafoya is one of the few Republicans in major races across the country who is outperforming expectations in the polls.

In August, Flanagan held an average lead of about seven points, but Tafoya has been closing the gap . More recent surveys suggest the race is essentially up for grabs. Still, a win by Tafoya would likely be considered a significant upset. Two of the most respected non-partisan elections forecasters — The Cook Political Report and The Center for Politics — list Minnesota's Senate race as a "likely" win for Democrats.

articles.title: Dem senator who demanded Saudi accountability over Khashoggi meets with crown prince, pushes Palestinian state
articles.summary: Chris Murphy met with Mohammed bin Salman to discuss ending the Iran war and establishing a Palestinian state, but notably avoided mentioning Jamal Khashoggi.
articles.body: A Senate Democrat pushing for an end to the war in Iran and the creation of a Palestinian state met with Saudi Arabia’s crown prince during a trip to the Middle East. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., in a post on X revealed that he had met with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, also known as MBS, on Monday. Murphy, who arrived in the region on Saturday for meetings in Qatar, acknowledged that he’s taken issue with the Saudi leader’s policies, but that it was "important for us to be here to recognize that there are things that we need to work on together — the end of the war with Iran, a pathway to a Palestinian state." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION UNVEILS SWEEPING TERMS OF PROPOSED IRAN AGREEMENT He noted that he’s been in disagreement with the Saudis, particularly over the Gulf country’s several investments in President Donald Trump’s family businesses, but that "there's got to be space for political dialogue and speech here in Saudi Arabia." "We talked about those things. I'm not saying we came to conclusions, but I think it's important for the crown prince to not just hear from the Trump administration, but to hear from people who want a different path for Saudi Arabia in the region and in the world," Murphy said. "But those points of alignment are important as well," he continued. "We are not going to get a permanent end to this war without the Saudis' help. We're not going to get a Palestinian state without the Saudis’ help." 4 GOP SENATORS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP ON IRAN WAR, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN AUTHORITY Murphy notably did not mention Jamal Khashoggi, a Washington Post journalist who was murdered and dismembered by Saudi operatives at a Saudi Arabian consulate in Turkey in 2018. Years ago, Murphy was demanding accountability from the Saudi government over Khashoggi’s slaying. "And I think what we have to remember is that it took two weeks for the Saudi government to cop to what had happened," Murphy said around the one-year anniversary of Khashoggi’s death. "The people that we do business with — the president and the secretary of state that talked to you on a regular basis — were lying to the entire world and to the American public for two weeks when it was patently clear as to what had happened." Fox News Digital reached out to Murphy’s office for comment on Khashoggi and his meeting with MBS. 'RED CARPET FOR A DESPOT': TRUMP'S LAVISH XI WELCOME COLLIDES WITH GOP ANTI-COMMUNISM MESSAGE Meanwhile, Murphy’s confab with MBS was part of a broader trip to the region. The lawmaker announced on Saturday that he had just arrived in Qatar for a slate of meetings and noted that he was likely the first Democrat to set foot in the Middle East since the Iran war began earlier this year. Murphy, one of the more vocal critics of the war, said his trip was meant to view war damage, speak with allies about the conflict’s regional impact and meet with actors working to end the fighting. He’s so far met with Ali Al Thawadi, a key diplomat who coordinates U.S.-Iran shuttle diplomacy, and another key leader in the region, Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Murphy noted that "there are so many things Qatar does to protect U.S. interests," like hosting the largest U.S. military base in the region, housing Afghan refugees, and acting as key middlemen to getting hostages out of Gaza. "And they are mediators right now in the effort to end the war with Iran," Murphy said. "I thanked him for all of this. Qatar is and will remain an essential ally of the United States." "Of course, I was also candid with him, in particular regarding my deep concerns about the transfer of the luxury plane," he continued.

articles.title: 'Honored': Talarico endorsed by group that bailed out violent criminal later accused of mass murder
articles.summary: US Senate candidate James Talarico praised activist group backing his campaign as 'irreplaceable' even though it freed a man who later killed six people in a mass murdering spree.
articles.body: Democratic U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico said he was "honored" to receive the endorsement of the Texas Organizing Project, whose work he described as "irreplaceable" after the organization previously operated a charitable bail fund that helped secure the release of Shane James — later accused of carrying out a six-person killing spree. The Texas Organizing Project (TOP), a progressive activist organization that endorsed Talarico's Senate campaign in May, previously operated a charitable bail program that, by September 2021, had distributed more than $1 million to secure the release of more than 675 defendants across Texas. The program drew intense scrutiny in late 2023 after authorities accused James of killing six people and records revealed that TOP had posted his bail nearly two years earlier while he faced three misdemeanor family-assault charges involving his parents and a sibling. UNEARTHED INTERVIEW EXPOSES WHAT TALARICO THOUGHT ABOUT 'TOUGH-ON-CRIME' TACTICS James cut off his court-ordered GPS monitor the day after his March 2022 release, prompting a court to issue three warrants for his re-arrest. Despite the outstanding warrants, James remained free for 21 months before authorities say he carried out a series of attacks across San Antonio and Austin that left six people dead, including his parents. TOP acknowledged after the killings that it had bailed James out in coordination with the Bexar County public defender's office after his bond was reduced to a combined $300. The organization said James had passed its screening process based on the misdemeanor charges he faced at the time and stressed that bail organizations cannot predict defendants' future behavior. "We acknowledge that our assessments cannot anticipate the future actions of individuals," TOP said following the killings, announcing that it would conduct an internal review of the program. Talarico nevertheless enthusiastically welcomed TOP's endorsement earlier this year. "I am honored to earn this endorsement," Talarico said when the group announced its backing, praising TOP for spending more than 15 years developing relationships in Black and Latino communities across Texas. "That infrastructure is irreplaceable," he said. PROGRESSIVE TALARICO KNIFES BIDEN'S OPEN BORDER, TRIES MODERATING STANCE ON KEY ISSUES IN TEXAS SENATE RACE The endorsement announcement said TOP members had met with Talarico before backing him, while the organization's leadership said the Senate candidate had demonstrated familiarity with its work. Talarico is challenging Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, as Democrats seek to break a decades-long losing streak in statewide Texas elections. Shane James was not the only defendant released through TOP's program who subsequently encountered additional legal trouble. A 2024 KSAT investigation found TOP had bonded defendants out in at least 196 Bexar County cases since jail officials began specifically tracking the organization's activity in October 2022. Warrants were later issued for defendants' re-arrest in 58 of those cases, or nearly 30%. While failure to appear in court was the most common reason for those warrants, records showed some defendants also faced new criminal charges after TOP secured their release. Among them was Benjamin Sanchez Jr., a convicted felon with two prior burglary convictions who TOP bonded out 11 days after his arrest in connection with the burglary of a San Antonio souvenir store. A warrant for Sanchez's re-arrest was later issued after pretrial violations that included his arrest on new burglary charges, according to KSAT. He ultimately pleaded guilty in the two newer burglary cases and was sentenced to six years in prison. TOP has defended its bail work as an effort to prevent low-income defendants from remaining incarcerated simply because they cannot afford bond. The organization said in 2021 that its Right2Justice campaign had spent more than $1 million to bail out more than 675 people, with the vast majority of the money distributed in Bexar County. TALARICO HIT WITH ‘BLATANT CORRUPTION’ ALLEGATION OVER HEFTY SALARY FROM CONSULTING FIRM, CAMPAIGN PUSHES BACK The organization's bail advocacy also intersected with Talarico's legislative record. TOP opposed HB 20 during the 2021 Texas legislative session, describing efforts to restrict community bail funds as part of a "right-wing assault" on the organizations. Talarico voted against a House version of HB 20 in May 2021, according to the Texas House Journal. Talarico's campaign pushed back on the significance of that vote in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing that the version he opposed differed substantially from the legislation ultimately considered later in the process, and pointing to his more recent support for tougher bail restrictions. "James will always work to keep Texans safe. That's why he voted to deny bail for violent criminals, supports prosecuting violent felons, and backed Governor Abbott's bill that was called the 'strongest bail reform package in Texas history,'" Talarico campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Fox News Digital. "The only candidate in this race endangering women and children is Ken Paxton, who cut an Epstein-style sweetheart deal that let a pedophile back on our streets after just 29 days in jail," Ennis added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The campaign pointed Fox News Digital to Talarico's 2025 vote for part of a bail reform package championed by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. The package included a constitutional amendment expanding the circumstances under which judges could deny bail to defendants accused of certain serious violent crimes. The campaign also argued that the 2021 House version of HB 20 that Talarico opposed contained broader provisions unrelated to charitable bail organizations, and noted criticism at the time that the proposal would continue allowing potentially dangerous defendants with sufficient money to secure their own release.

articles.title: America’s new blue-collar job boom is one nobody saw coming — and it’s just getting started
articles.summary: Compass Datacenters CEO Chris Crosby says the Red Oak, Texas, campus proves data centers need electricians, welders and carpenters over degrees.
articles.body: Red Oak, Texas — Inside a sprawling Texas data center campus, blinking tower lights and rows of neatly organized cables power the technology Americans use every day. Keeping it all running, however, takes an army of electricians, mechanics, technicians and construction workers — and the industry says it needs more of them. "Unfortunately, there was a war on blue-collar jobs a while back and everybody had to get a four-year degree. I’m so glad that’s over with," Compass Datacenters CEO Chris Crosby told Fox News Digital while giving a glimpse behind the scenes of the infrastructure that powers the digital world. "I am tired of the elitism that this doesn't create jobs," Crosby said, arguing that blue-collar careers deserve to be taken seriously. He pointed to the workers at Compass’s Red Oak campus and the construction crews who built it. "You tell that to the 900 people who work here on this campus and you tell that to the thousands of construction workers who have worked here for five years plus," he said. A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES Compass began developing its Red Oak campus, about 20 miles south of Dallas, in 2019. The site now includes 10 data center buildings totaling about 2.6 million square feet, a Schneider Electric manufacturing facility and a technical college training program. Crosby said more than 600 people work full time at the campus, with roughly 300 more at Schneider Electric. The construction also requires a range of skilled tradespeople, Crosby said. "When we look at that type of opportunity, the amount of electricians, the amount of mechanical contractors, the number of builders, the carpenters, the welders, the concrete folk, it’s awesome. We can’t get enough people into this career." INSIDE THE NEIGHBORHOOD LIVING ON THE EDGE OF AMERICA’S TECH FRONTIER The demand also reaches beyond construction sites to factories producing data center components. Compass and its partners, Crosby said, have created more than 7,000 permanent factory jobs nationwide. To help meet the industry’s demand for workers, Compass partnered with Texas State Technical College to build a $12.6 million training facility at its Red Oak campus. The company created its MEI Pathways program—short for Mechanical, Electrical and IT Pathways—to prepare people for those careers. "The big challenge is how do I get the first step?" Crosby said. "That’s what MEI Pathways is designed to do." The program is open to anyone interested in the field and does not require prior qualifications, Crosby said. It is designed to train workers for the broader industry, not just for Compass. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Crosby said building that workforce will be increasingly important as data centers expand and argued that the facilities can bring jobs and tax revenue to the communities where they are built. "Data centers are where the economic engine is going to be going forward," he said. "You’re talking about massive amounts of jobs, economic activity and tax revenue growth."

articles.title: Supreme Court begins new term with high-profile look at clean air and federal authority
articles.summary: The Supreme Court heard arguments on whether Boulder County's climate lawsuit against Suncor and ExxonMobil belongs in state or federal court.
articles.body: The Supreme Court launched its new term Monday with a blockbuster oral argument over whether federal or state laws and courts should handle civil lawsuits against energy companies for alleged climate change harms. Eight justices debated for nearly two hours on a key gateway over environmental liability — who decides and where. It was unclear after the public session how the court might rule. Absent was Justice Samuel Alito, who recused last week after calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies, but not the two at the center of Monday's appeal. Local and state governments seek civil damages totaling billions of dollars, arguing it is necessary to help pay for rebuilding after wildfires, rising sea levels, and severe storms worsened by fossil fuel pollution. SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA Colorado's highest court let the case brought by Boulder County proceed. SUPREME COURT SIDES WITH CHEVRON, OIL COMPANIES IN LOUISIANA ENVIRONMENTAL LAWSUITS The companies — backed by the Trump administration — counter emissions are a national issue that should be heard in federal court, where similar suits have been tossed out. The justices will also decide whether they have jurisdiction to hear this dispute, or whether it belongs in state courts. SUPREME COURT CLIMATE SHOWDOWN JOLTED BY ALITO'S LAST-MINUTE DECISION Chief Justice John Roberts could be the deciding vote. He asked tough questions of both sides and his vote could produce a 4-4 tie with Alito not participating. That would mean the specific lawsuit moves ahead in state courts. He said the court in the past has allowed similar claims to be decided outside the federal venue. WAVE OF OVERLOOKED 'LEFT-WING' LAWSUITS COULD COME WITH AN UNEXPECTED PRICE TAG FOR AMERICANS "There are a lot of familiar situations where conduct outside of the state has broad effects among other states, and yet we allow state courts in a particular state to bring litigation," said Roberts. "I guess I'm not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones, where we've allowed them to proceed in state court." Justice Elena Kagan compared the climate change lawsuits to previous claims against tobacco and opioid companies brought by states on behalf of their citizens. THE SUPREME COURT IS BACK. THESE FIVE CASES COULD RESHAPE AMERICAN LIFE "This is the same kind of lawsuit against the same kind of actors for the same kind of harm," said Kagan. "Where does this principle come from, that states can't regulate in the air and water space?" But Justice Brett Kavanaugh seemed to speak for many of his conservative colleagues, on the implications for multi-jurisdictional lawsuits to play out, potentially for decades. " It is going to bankrupt – if there are enough of these [lawsuits] — bankrupt these various defendants and certainly other defendants out there. Anyone is a potential defendant for a suit like this. Any manufacturer, any business," suggested Kavanaugh. "We don't have to reinvent the wheel because we've said this multiple times," he added, "and Congress, presumably, when doing the Clean Air Act and doing the Clean Air Act amendments, has relied on this Court's precedents establishing that this kind of pollution is a federal law matter unless Congress speaks otherwise." The current litigation is part of dozens of lawsuits brought by states and municipalities across the country. Boulder County, located north-west of Denver, sued in 2018. Among the defendants is Suncor, a Canadian-based energy giant that operates the only major oil refinery in Colorado. ExxonMobil, the largest oil company in the U.S., is also a defendant. Local officials claim the energy firms have misled the public about their role in climate change, and say financial penalties are necessary to mitigate ongoing harms in their communities, including recent forest fires and worsening air pollution. Some states also accuse the current administration of rolling back mandated protections in the Clean Air Act and thereby abdicating their regulatory authority. But the companies and the Trump Justice Department argue climate change should be addressed by the national government in federal court, and that the Clean Air Act limits what individual states and counties can do. FOLLOW US ON X They say this global problem is not limited to any one energy sector or country, and cannot be resolved by what they call local "power grabs." Some litigators believe the companies could fare better in federal court since they would not have to juggle dozens of ongoing lawsuits in multiple jurisdictions. "Interstate air pollution is an inherently federal area," Sarah Harris, a Justice Department lawyer, told the court. "This suit egregiously exceeds constitutional limits on state authority," Harris told the justices. CLICK HERE FOR MORE U.S. NEWS With the possibility of an evenly divided court, the eight justices may not have to reach the merits of the federalism question. GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS The Supreme Court specifically asked both parties to address at argument whether it should even hear the case, at least at this stage. That procedural "exit ramp" could put the larger issues off for another day. "I understand that you have several other federal issues that you have raised that are still pending in the state court," Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson asked the oil companies lawyer Kannon Shanmugam. "So why shouldn't we wait and hear all of these claims once the state courts are done with their federal considerations?" The case is Suncor Energy Inc. v. Commissioners of Boulder County, CO (25-170). CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A decision is expected by next spring.

articles.title: White House removes Politico from press pool for Trump’s trip to Nebraska
articles.summary: The administration took similar action last week against CNN. The cable news network, MS NOW and Politico sued after they were banned from the White House grounds.
articles.body: The White House prohibited Politico on Monday from traveling on Air Force One with President Donald Trump as he heads to Nebraska for a campaign rally. The move comes amid a legal fight between the Trump administration and several news organizations. “Many outlets including Politico are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right,” a White House official said in a statement. CNN first reported the administration’s action against Politico. The White House last month banned Politico, CNN and MS NOW from entering the White House, with Trump saying on Truth Social that the move was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” A federal judge last month ordered the administration to temporarily restore their access, but the order was limited to the White House grounds. Politico and a lawyer representing the three news outlets in their lawsuit against the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment Monday. The White House last week removed CNN from the press pool set to cover Trump’s trip to Texas and Oklahoma. The White House press pool consists of media outlets that share video, editorial information and costs for coverage of high-profile officials and events involving the president anywhere in the world. Under the system, designated “poolers” represent the wider press corps each day to document newsworthy events and serve as a conduit between the president and the public. The White House press corps has separate print, radio, still photography and TV pools. Politico was set to serve as the print travel pool Monday. A pool note from CBS News, which is handling the TV pool for the day, said the White House was unable to find a news outlet to replace Politico. After CNN was restricted from administration events last month, the four other member networks of the press pool — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — declined to participate in pool duties in solidarity. CBS on Monday said it would share its TV pool notes — which are usually distributed internally among the five pool networks — with the White House Correspondents’ Association. The network noted it was not replacing Politico as the print pool. The White House Correspondents’ Association, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and a group of 49 news and media organizations that included NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, filed a legal brief last month in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

articles.title: Biden-era FBI tracked Trump family travel and Wiles’ calls with lawyers in secret probe: docs
articles.summary: Declassified records reveal the Biden-era FBI tracked Melania and Barron Trump's travel while planning the Mar-a-Lago classified documents search.
articles.body: The Biden-era FBI tracked First Lady Melania Trump and Barron Trump's travel, while surveilling President Trump's future Chief of Staff Susie Wiles' phone, as officials worked the classified documents investigation reaching deep into Trump's inner circle, newly declassified records show. Documents released Monday by the White House detail "Plasmic Echo," the probe later led by special counsel Jack Smith into whether Trump improperly retained classified documents after leaving office. The declassified documents show agents tracked the First Lady and First Son's travel while planning the Mar-a-Lago search, then monitored Susie Wiles’ calls involving defense lawyers, campaign advisers and journalists. The surveillance collected call details rather than conversation contents, according to the documents. TOP INVESTIGATOR IN BIDEN-ERA ELECTION PROBE WANTED TO TEAR KEY CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT AWAY FROM LAWMAKERS "Jack Smith’s surveillance operation was a disgraceful abuse of government power. Spying on political opponents is weaponization of law enforcement, plain and simple," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "Those responsible must be held accountable." The revelations come less than a week after Smith faced a contentious Senate Judiciary Committee hearing over investigative tactics used in his separate probe into Trump's efforts to challenge the 2020 election. articles.title: 3 takeaways from our new poll of Latino voters: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Scott Bland breaks down the key numbers to know from our new national poll of the Latino electorate. Plus, Sahil Kapur dives into Democrats’ lingering divisions over transgender issues. — Adam Wollner 3 takeaways from our new poll of Latino voters Analysis by Scott Bland Latino voters’ swing toward President Donald Trump was one of the defining trends of the 2024 election. Their swing back could define the 2026 midterms, too. That’s the broad takeaway from the NBC News/Telemundo poll that came out Sunday, which showed Democrats with a 24-point lead among Latino registered voters on a 2026 ballot test. That’s a double-digit turnaround from the 2024 edition of the survey — and it comes after Republicans in Florida and Texas made big redistricting bets on extending the party’s results in the last election. Here are three big takeaways from the numbers: The economy is the driving factor. Immigration and border security are still important to many Latino voters, but their top issue is the cost of living, and Trump’s inability to follow through on his campaign promise to lower prices is biting his party. Latino voters gave Trump a 4-percentage-point edge over Kamala Harris in 2024 on who they thought would do a better job handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question. That’s a big reason almost a quarter (22%) of Latino Trump voters said they’re not planning to back Republicans in the midterms, with 14% choosing Democrats and 8% undecided from that group. Visceral feelings on immigration. Again, it’s not a leading issue when voters have to rank them, but Latino voters have strong feelings about Trump’s immigration agenda. Two-thirds say his enforcement policies have gone too far. Only 39% approve of his handling of border security and 30% approve on immigration overall. Meanwhile, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying ID because of concerns about getting swept up by ICE enforcement operations, and 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE since Trump’s second term began. There were key differences across gender, region and more. Just like in the overall electorate, Latino women lean more Democratic than Latino men. And while the sample was small, Latino voters from Florida were less likely to back Democrats than Latino voters elsewhere — something to keep in mind on election night, when it would be unwise to expect uniform swings from 2024 across different regions. ➡️ Related read: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas, by Natasha Korecki Trump-district Democrats draw blowback from Human Rights Campaign over trans rhetoric By Sahil Kapur The country’s largest LGBTQ rights group is criticizing some Democrats who are adopting what they see as anti-transgender rhetoric in their campaigns, a point of tension as the party wrestles with how to handle the issue heading into the 2026 election. They include Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, who said in a recent ad, “I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls’ sports.” They also include Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., who is similarly running in a red-leaning district that Donald Trump carried in the last election. In a recent ad, Davis cited a North Carolina law that prohibits trans women and girls from playing on female sports teams, saying there are “real concerns about fairness and safety” for “women and girls in sports.” Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson told reporters today that those candidates are “doing too much and getting too little” with their strategies. “You don’t have to sacrifice any member of our community to win in these races, to have a message that resonates with voters,” Robinson said at a breakfast in Washington. “You’ve got Marcy Kaptur, who not only is bad on the message, but she’s also bad on the policy. I mean, she voted for a bill that would have put forced outing in place nationally. A don’t-say-trans bill, too, right? She’s somebody that hasn’t been with us on either of those sides, so she’s not someone that we’re supporting this cycle,” Robinson said. Meanwhile, Robinson praised former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who is running again for the Senate in Ohio. Brown has sought to reframe the debate, featuring a voter in an ad who says: “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” “Sherrod Brown, on the other hand, I think, did a great job in his response ad that we worked with him pretty closely on — in stating what the laws are in Ohio now and reaffirming his support from the community and then, most importantly, letting voters talk for themselves,” Robinson said. In light of the criticism, Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer said in a statement: “Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls’ sports stay fair. She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor.” A Davis spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Meanwhile, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has not advised 2026 candidates to take any particular approach on trans issues, according to a person familiar with the committee’s thinking, who said it is “supportive of each candidate messaging as they see fit” in their districts while simply encouraging them to “explain to voters where they stand.” Where the Human Rights Campaign and the Democrats they are criticizing agree is that the GOP attacks are effective if left unanswered. But they disagree over how to answer them. Robinson argued that the “core failure” of Democrats and Kamala Harris in 2024 was “the lack of a direct response.” She said of 2026: “We’ve given counsel and guidance that’s really very clear. Address the attack head-on, pivot to your values — the things that you want voters to know about.” A Democratic strategist involved in 2026 races said that is one school of thought, which can be effective in message testing. Another school of thought, said the strategist, is to directly confront the attacks and seek distance on the issue in order to “not look like a typical Democrat.” The latter approach “works better as your district gets redder,” said the strategist, who was not authorized to discuss internal machinations on the record. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Trump’s approval hits new low among Hispanic voters ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Hispanic voters are twice as likely to favour Democratic Party over Trump’s Republican Party in the November elections.
articles.body:
A new poll from the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos has found that United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating remains at a record low as the midterm elections approach in November.

The six-day survey, completed on Monday, found that just 32 percent of US voters approve of the job Trump is doing as president.

While that low rate has held steady since September, the latest Reuters-Ipsos poll suggests his support among Latino voters is continuing to slide.

Trump’s approval rating shrunk this month to 24 percent among Hispanic voters , its lowest point in either of his two terms in office.

The Republican leader had previously made substantial inroads with that constituency.

The Pew Research Center estimated that Trump and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were within three percentage points of each other in the 2024 presidential race, earning 48 percent and 51 percent of the Hispanic vote, respectively.

That rate marked a significant jump for Trump over the 2020 election, when he only earned 36 percent of the Hispanic vote.

Experts have credited the boost in Hispanic support with helping Trump win the 2024 race. His 2020 bid, by contrast, ended in defeat to Democrat Joe Biden.

The Monday poll found that Trump’s gains among Hispanics have largely evaporated.

About 52 percent plan to vote for the Democrats in the November midterms, compared to 26 percent for Republicans.

The upcoming midterm is largely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second term and will decide whether the Republicans maintain their majorities in the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Democrats have seized on Trump’s low approval ratings, hoping to translate frustration with the president into voter momentum for their party.

A Democratic majority in one or both houses of Congress would place substantial constraints on Trump’s agenda for the remainder of his time in office.

But Trump has also faced rumblings from within his Republican Party as the November 3 midterms approach.

One Republican incumbent, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, released a campaign advertisement last month that addressed Trump directly, saying, “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

She cited Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown as a source of tension. “Some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said, pointing to the detention and deportation of immigrants with no criminal record.

Experts have also warned that the president’s shrinking popularity, driven in part by concerns about the cost of living and his decision to launch a war on Iran , could weigh down Republican candidates in key races across the country.

Still, Trump has continued to express confidence about the prospects of his Republican Party in the upcoming midterms.

He has also defended his decision to place himself at the centre of the Republican election campaign strategy. Trump recently launched a 32-day blitz of cross-country rallies ahead of the November 3 midterms.

“Just so you understand, they all want me to go,” Trump said, denying that some Republicans would prefer he keep his distance. “They all want me to go campaign.”

articles.body:
President Trump on Monday used an anti-transgender slur several times against Sen. Darline Graham’s (R-S.C.) Democratic opponent Dr. Annie Andrews, as the race for South Carolina’s Senate seat tightens.

“Annie ‘T——‘ Andrews is running against our wonderful Darline Graham for the Senate in South Carolina,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

The president evoked Graham’s late brother and Senate predecessor, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), to praise her loyalty and describe her as “the finest, most reliable and one of the smartest people I have ever known.” Trump quipped that when the former senator would say these things, it would upset the president “because I thought I had all of those qualities.”

“In any event, Darline is a High Quality person, maybe the Highest, and Annie T—— is not, in particular, as it pertains to representing the Values of the Great People of South Carolina — She is in favor of Transgender for Everyone, Open Borders, Defunding the Police, High Taxes, a Weak Military, and will absolutely fight to take your guns away — In other words, she is against our Great Second Amendment!” Trump continued.

He used the slur again in saying that Andrews is “not for South Carolina” before calling on voters to choose Graham.

Andrews, a pediatrician and mother of three, told The Hill after Trump’s post went live that she’s “in this race to fight for my patients, my three kids and South Carolina.”

“And I’m going to work with anyone to put South Carolina first, because lowering costs and making life better for families across our state is going to take all of us working together,” she said in a statement. “If you care more about your bills than the politics in Washington, this campaign is for you.”

If Andrews wins in November, she will become the first pediatrician elected senator, the outlet Motherly wrote as part of an interview with Andrews published in May .

“I want my kids to know they are capable of doing anything they put their minds to,” she told the outlet. “That every fight is worth fighting no matter how difficult it seems. I want them to know I am doing this for them. That they give me the strength I need to keep going.”

Andrews has campaigned on reversing Trump’s policies that have caused prices to soar — in particular healthcare and children’s healthcare costs, The New York Times reported . But she has also softened some of her past campaign positions, including on transgender issues, as she faces a widespread and largely conservative electorate.

She previously said she was against a bill to ban transgender athletes from girls and women’s sports but told the Times that she does not “support biological men playing in women’s sports.”

Election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted the race from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican,” pointing to Graham’s debate flub on foreign policy and Andrews’s low polling numbers. The report credited Andrews with “running a real race” and said this help could make it “a truly competitive contest.”

A Republican official told the Times that Trump plans to campaign for Graham later this month.

articles.body:
Appeals court to hear lawsuit against RFK Jr. vaccine moves

A federal appeals court will hear arguments Tuesday in a lawsuit filed by medical groups against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, seeking to block his overhaul of the childhood vaccine schedule .

© Jose Luis Magana, Associated Press file

In January, Kennedy and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) made sweeping changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, reducing the number of recommended diseases to be vaccinated against from 18 to 11. The CDC also dropped universal recommendations that all babies should be vaccinated against hepatitis A, hepatitis B, RSV, dengue and two types of bacterial meningitis.

Kennedy also fired and replaced every member of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices with people highly skeptical of vaccines.

Medical groups led by the American Academy of Pediatrics, including the American College of Physicians and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, sued. The lawsuit claimed the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and the changes were made arbitrarily and capriciously .

A district court judge initially ruled in their favor and temporarily blocked changes to the childhood vaccine schedule and paused any decisions made by the committee, ruling that Kennedy replaced the members “unlawfully.”

According to the medical groups, changes to vaccine recommendations should be made only with scientific justification . Any efforts to degrade the current recommendations could lead to reduced coverage, increased vaccination hesitancy, increased risk of the spread of preventable diseases, and increased mortality.

The Trump administration appealed, and a hearing on that appeal is set for Tuesday in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First District.

articles.title: Tillis calls Hegseth vote his ‘biggest regret’
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) wrote in his upcoming book that he views his confirmation vote for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the “biggest regret” of his career. Tillis’s upcoming memoir — “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” which will hit the shelves Tuesday — breaks down how he was skeptical of allegations made about…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) wrote in his upcoming book that he views his confirmation vote for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the “biggest regret” of his career.

Tillis’s upcoming memoir — “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” which will hit the shelves Tuesday — breaks down how he was skeptical of allegations made about Hegseth’s treatment of women, style of management and excessive drinking, The Associated Press reported . But he said he chose not to be “the lone voice in the wilderness.”

“I know for a fact that there are others like me, Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far,” Tillis wrote.

Tillis pushed the confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he spoke with the White House, people who worked with Hegseth and the nominee himself, the AP reported. He ultimately failed to corroborate the worst of the allegations against the former Fox News host, siding with Republicans.

At the time of the vote, he said he conducted his “due diligence” to ask Hegseth “tough questions.”

“Pete has a unique perspective as a veteran of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and is unquestionably passionate about modernizing our military and supporting the brave patriots like himself who serve our nation,” he said in a January 2025 statement . “I will support his confirmation and look forward to working with him to rebuild our military and advance President Trump’s peace through strength agenda.”

The North Carolina Republican, who has been a vocal critic of some of the president’s policies and proposals and who will be leaving Congress at the end of his term, has suggested that he would not have confirmed Hegseth, but said in July 2025 that he did not regret the decision.

Last month, Tillis said he backed an impeachment resolution against Hegseth.

“He needs to go, whether it’s impeachment or the most expedient route — just the president to replace him — would be great,” he told reporters.

The memoir also delves into Tillis’s regret over confirming Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., among other Cabinet officials he criticizes in the book, the AP wrote.

“I guess it’s easy to say now, but I’m the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy’s tenure has caused the country as a result,” Tillis wrote about the secretary.

He predicted a “bloodbath” for Republicans looking to keep and expand their majorities in Congress after the November midterm elections, and he deflected full blame from Trump. He wrote that he does not have “beef” with the president, “but the idiots he’s got working for him.”
