articles.title: Trump clears way for Fort Hood terrorist to face Army firing squad nearly 17 years after massacre
articles.summary: President Trump cleared the way for Nidal Malik Hasan to face an Army firing squad nearly 17 years after the Fort Hood massacre that killed 13 people.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has cleared the way for the Fort Hood terrorist to face an Army firing squad, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell announced Monday, nearly 17 years after a deadly rampage. "Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," Parnell wrote on X. "He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting 'Allahu Akbar' during the attack. " Nidal Malik Hasan, a former army officer, killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in the 2009 attack at Fort Hood, shouting "Allahu Akbar" as he opened fire. Where the death penalty has been used before and since that attack, Hasan's death, if carried out, will mark the first time a president has successfully signed off on a U.S. military execution since 1961, a penalty reserved for members of the U.S. military as the gravest use of a court-marshal under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. FOX FILES TAKES AN IN-DEPTH LOOK AT FORT HOOD KILLINGS Pvt. John Bennett was last executed by hanging on April 13, 1961, after he attempted to murder an 11-year-old girl in Austria. President George W. Bush also approved of a military execution but was stopped by a federal court in 2008. In Hasan's case, he took a pistol and a 0.357 revolver with him to a mosque where he attended noon prayers. He then drove to a a soldier readiness processing facility, an administrative building, full of what Hasan knew were going to be unarmed soldiers. After shouting "Allahu Akbar," Hasan unloaded into "the greatest density of soldiers," according to witness statements. "I shot to kill," Hasan told the Sanity Board report. Hasan was eventually detained after engaging in a fire fight with law enforcement, sustaining multiple gun wounds. He was apprehended and rushed to intensive care. According to the sanity report, he denied experiencing depressive, manic, psychotic, anxiety or cognitive symptoms during the attack. Hasan was court marshaled four years later and sentenced to death. ALLEGED FORT HOOD SHOOTER FREQUENTED LOCAL STRIP CLUB "In Hasan's sentencing, lead prosecutor Col. Michael Mulligan rested the government's case on the morning of Aug. 27, after two days of emotional testimony from surviving widows and parents of some of those murdered, Nov. 5, 2009," the Army's press release stated. "One of the witnesses, Joleen Cahill, said her husband, retired Chief Warrant Officer Michael Cahill, had given his life in an effort to stop Hasan. She spoke of the devastation experienced by her family in the time following the shooting." As a part of the press release, the Ford Hood Public Affairs Office explained that Hasan's case would be automatically appealed, a part of the process for any death sentence. "Given that the death sentence was imposed, the military justice system requires this case to be automatically appealed to the U.S. Army Criminal Court of Appeals and then to the United States Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces," the press release added. After a court upheld the death sentence in early 2025, representation for Hasan appealed to the Supreme Court, citing procedural objections to how the trial was run, but that review was denied. With President Trump's approval, the Army secretary will set the execution's time and place, Parnell, the Pentagon spokesperson, said. "Judgment day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.

articles.title: After bipartisan criticism, Trump says taxpayers’ dollars will no longer be used for TV ads promoting him
articles.summary: The president said the ads, which the White House has defended, will be funded by him and his super PAC, MAGA Inc.
articles.body: In a major reversal, President Donald Trump said Monday that he and his super PAC will now pay for campaign-style ads that promote his administration, instead of using federal funds. Trump made the announcement on Truth Social after intense criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, some of whom questioned the legality of using taxpayer dollars for pro-Trump ads. “The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.” Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., did not immediately respond to an inquiry about whether Trump and it would reimburse the government for the ads that have already aired. The White House did not answer that question, either. “MAGA Inc. will pay for the PSA ads moving forward,” a White House official said. “Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction,” the official added. AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, estimated the government has spent at least $10 million to air the ads. The ads, which portray Trump in a favorable light, included disclaimers saying they were paid for by the U.S. government. One of the spots was virtually identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad. NBC News reported last week that the ads were paid for by money intended for U.S. Customs and Border Protection, but senior leaders at the agency were cut out of the decision. A Maryland-based firm, LMD Agency, was awarded a $20 million contract for the new ads, according to public contracting records. The purpose of the contract was listed as a “national media campaign.” Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have condemned the ads. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called it “propaganda,” while Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, likened Trump to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. “There’s no place for that sort of thing,” Tillis said. The White House previously defended the ads, calling them “clearly not political” and saying the PSAs were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”

articles.title: Trump uses anti-trans slur against Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina
articles.summary: Annie Andrews is a physician running against Sen. Darline Graham.
articles.body: President Donald Trump used an anti-trans slur Monday to attack the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina as he urged voters to back Republican Sen. Darline Graham. In a Truth Social post, Trump referred to Democratic candidate Annie Andrews three times as “trannie.” He said Andrews, who is not transgender, is “not for South Carolina.” “And South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her,” Trump added. Andrews responded by largely ignoring the insult, saying in a statement first shared with NBC News that she will “work with anyone to put South Carolina first.” “As a mom and a pediatrician, I’m in this race to fight for my patients, my three kids, and South Carolina,” Andrews said, adding that “lowering costs and making life better for families across our state is going to take all of us working together.” “If you care more about your bills than the politics in Washington, this campaign is for you,” she said. Graham’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the post by Trump, who often uses insulting nicknames for politicians and officials he dislikes. Reached for comment on why Trump used the slur, the White House referred NBC News to his social media post. The Human Rights Campaign, an LGBTQ advocacy organization, blasted Trump’s remarks, calling them “the sad, disgusting, pathetic diatribes of a lame duck president with record-low approvals.” “So low, in fact, he’s having to campaign in deep red territory in a desperate attempt to shore up support ahead of the midterms,” Ramiro Sarmiento, a spokesperson for the organization, said in a statement. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., condemned Trump’s words Monday night, calling his attacks on Andrews “despicable.” “Annie Andrews is a mom and pediatrician who’s always put her community first — and she’s exactly who South Carolina needs representing them in the Senate,” Schumer said on X. Andrews, a physician, has previously said she does not support gender-affirming surgery for minors or transgender athletes’ participating in women’s sports. Former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley, a Republican, criticized the president for his attack on Andrews, asking voters to “reject politics based on division and hate.” “This is abhorrent. Elections don’t have to be about cruelty and lies. South Carolina deserves better,” Beasley wrote Monday night on X. Graham is running to keep her seat after Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to fill her late brother’s seat after Lindsey Graham died in July. Graham won the Republican primary in a runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman by nearly 5 percentage points. She has leaned heavily on Trump’s endorsement to make her case to South Carolina. While South Carolina has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly three decades, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race toward Democrats last month, moving it from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.”

articles.title: Dennis Hastert, longest-serving Republican House Speaker and convicted child molester, dies at 84
articles.summary: The Mark Foley scandal nearly ended Dennis Hastert's career, but federal investigators later uncovered far darker secrets about the former House Speaker.
articles.body: The late House Speaker Dennis Hastert (R-IL) was an accidental speaker. And it was a sheer accident that the world learned a dark secret about Hastert, years after he left Capitol Hill. It was twenty years ago, almost to the date. House Republicans were on the verge of losing their majority in the 2006 midterms. And their Speaker, Dennis Hastert, was in meltdown. HIGHEST-RANKING US OFFICIAL TO EVER SERVE JAIL TIME, FORMER HOUSE SPEAKER DENNIS HASTERT DEAD AT 84 Word had just broken that then-Rep. Mark Foley (R-FL) had sent inappropriate messages to high school-age male teens, serving as House pages. The Republican-led House was meeting on September 29, 2006, trying to escape town so the GOP could defend their majority. But nothing was going right for Republicans. The public was growing weary of President George W. Bush and the war in Iraq. Democrats were poised to retake the House in November. Yours truly and Deirdre Walsh — then of CNN — spotted the portly Hastert lumbering across Statuary Hall toward the Speaker’s office. "Did he call you?" Walsh asked Hastert about Foley. "What are you going to do about it?" I inquired. "We’ll talk about that shortly," mumbled Hastert under his breath, his wide glasses nearly tumbling over the bridge of his nose as he huffed into the Speaker’s suite. An hour later, Hastert, outgoing Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist (R-TN) and other top Republicans convened a brief press conference to tout a national security bill they just passed. The legislation was designed as the GOP sendoff as lawmakers went home to campaign. "Ok, we’ll take questions. Only on the bill," instructed Frist. "Only on the bill." No one even squeaked. Finally, I piped up. "We have questions about other subjects," I announced, determined to ask about Foley. "Alright," said Frist, shoving back from the table. The Tennessee Republican knew what was coming. Frist was happy he wouldn’t have to address Foley. That was something for Hastert. Especially since Frist planned to run for President in 2008. I inquired about Foley. Hastert muttered a non-answer which was barely usable for broadcast. He mumbled something about him not being "very happy" about Foley. But it was a soundbite from the Speaker of the House on the scandal, right as a bloodied GOP hit the exits for the midterm campaign. Someone then quickly adjourned the press conference. And that was it. FORMER REPUBLICAN HOUSE SPEAKER DENNIS HASTERT DEAD AT 84 A few days later, local reporters in Illinois pressed Hastert about how he handled the Foley matter. Back in Washington, asked one of the Speaker’s aides why Hastert – as a former teacher and coach – wasn’t more aggressive protecting the teen pages. We may have found out why years later. Eighty-four year-old Dennis Hastert died of natural causes over the weekend. The late Speaker is one of the most ignominious figures in American politics. He was the longest-serving Republican Speaker in history, wielding the gavel from 1999 to 2007. Hastert stumbled into the Speakership, rising thanks to the missteps of others. Yet despite his years in Congress, what we learned about Hastert nearly a decade after he left office revealed him to be one of the most grotesque persons to ever serve in Congress. In fact, Hastert is the highest-serving U.S. official to ever serve jail time. Virtually no one knew it, but Hastert was an unbridled sexual predator. Known as "Coach" rather than "Mr. Speaker" to his Capitol colleagues, Hastert preyed on teenage boys when he taught high school in the 1960s and 1970s. Hastert was never implicated in the page scandal. The House nixed the program soon afterwards, even though it was nearly as old as the republic. But in retrospect, how Hastert fumbled what was going on with the House pages shockingly added up later. Democrats won the House handily in the 2006 midterms. Hastert didn’t run – and probably wouldn’t have won – a leadership race in the new Congress. He stuck around as rank-and-file member for a few months and resigned in late 2007. Few heard much from Hastert after he departed Congress. Such was his style. He shunned interviews as Speaker and was rarely even spotted in the Capitol corridors. To defend his reticence with the press corps, the Speaker proclaimed that he was more of a "listener." And then Hastert’s otherwise bland, nearly forgotten Speakership took a dark turn in 2015. Federal banking regulators flagged Hastert’s curious withdrawals of staggering amounts of cash. They suspected the transactions signaled that someone could be blackmailing the former Speaker. So they investigated. But that’s how it came to light that Hastert was actually paying hush money to conceal his sexual transgressions with minors. The feds indicted Hastert on charges of lying to investigators and evading banking laws. He later pleaded guilty to the bank crimes. Prosecutors dropped the charge of making false statements. Federal Judge Thomas Durkin declared that the former Speaker was "a serial child molester." In court, Hastert admitted that he "mistreated athletes" and "took advantage" of those he was supposed to mentor. Prosecutors never charged Hastert in connection with sex crimes. He served 13 months of a 15-month sentence at a federal facility in Rochester, MN. It’s remarkable that someone who operated at this level of American government obscured such a hideous secret for so long. And as instructive as the day nearly 20 years ago when the Foley scandal broke and Republicans were on the verge of losing the House, unceremoniously terminating Hastert’s Speakership — the day that propelled him into the leadership is even more illuminating. Republicans nearly lost the House in the 1998 midterms. House Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-GA) was toxic and Republicans showed him the door. In late 1998, Republicans tapped then-Rep. Bob Livingston (R-LA), chairmanof the Appropriations Committee, to become Speaker in 1999. But then came December 19, 1998. The Saturday before Christmas. I was on the job on 9/11. I was on the job on January 6. I’ve covered Congress for a litany of big hearings, the removal of House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-CA). Even the day they banished Pete Rose from Major League Baseball as a kid reporter back in Cincinnati. You name it, I’ve seen it. But from a sheer news perspective, December 19, 1998 rivals many of those. The House met on that Saturday before Christmas to approve articles of impeachment against President Clinton for the Monica Lewinsky scandal. This would mark only the second time in American history that the House impeached an American President. President Clinton also ordered airstrikes against Iraq for violating no-fly zones following the first Gulf War that day. So that story was in full force. But the night before, there was news that Livingston – the GOP’s Speaker in waiting – had an affair with a lobbyist. Juxtapose that with what the House was trying to do with Clinton because of his sexual exploits. On the morning of December 19, 1998, Livingston took to the House floor to demand that the president resign for his transgressions. "No! You resign! You resign!" came a cacophony of catcalls from Democrats in unison in the House chamber. Livingston paused and held up his hand to quiet the din. The Louisiana Republican then announced he would not stand as the GOP’s nominee for Speaker when the new Congress convened in January 1999. He promised to resign from the House a few months later. FOLLOW US ON X Bedlam tore through the Capitol. House Republicans scrambled. They needed a new Speaker-designee. By nightfall, they conscripted J. Dennis Hastert for the job. The Chief Deputy Whip in the Republican Conference. Hastert was a part of the GOP leadership team. But he was a backbencher. His obscure leadership slot was to help count votes on the floor. Many reporters who covered Congress didn’t even know who Hastert was. Hastert was barely vetted by the press corps. But there was other big news. Airstrikes against Iraq. The Livingston scandal. That’s to say nothing of only the second impeachment trial of a President in American history. GOT A TIP? Hastert seized the Speaker’s gavel in January 1999. He remained on the job for another eight years. Longer than any other Republican. His odious past obscured. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But ultimately, Dennis Hastert did not take to the grave the loathsome secrets he hid for so long.

articles.title: Trump says he will pay for ‘Patriotic Ads’ himself after facing backlash from Democrats
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday said he will pay for the controversial “Patriotic Ads” after backlash mounted in response to the ads being funded by taxpayers. “The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with…
articles.body:
President Trump on Monday said he will pay for the controversial “ Patriotic Ads ” after backlash mounted in response to the ads being funded by taxpayers.

“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” the president added.

The $20-million ad campaign features Trump in a voiceover claiming the U.S. will defeat socialism and communism while also saying the country is “reigniting American manufacturing” under his presidency.

Trump’s voice says he and his followers “will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” referring to the press and his political opponents, as “Love Me” by JMSN, the moniker of singer Christian Berishaj, plays in the background.

The ads are not intended for any campaign, as they do not promote any specific candidate or political party. Trump has previously pushed back against the criticism by saying that they are fair game for not outwardly supporting him, claiming that they are for the “spirit of the country.”

Vice President Vance also defended the ads , saying that there’s a history where the federal government has used tax dollars to promote government actions, using the Obama administration’s ads for the Affordable Care Act as an example. Trump halted that effort at the start of his first term.

“It’s part of actually, I think, living in a constitutional republic,” Vance told reporters Monday. “You have to be honest with the American people about what you’re doing, about what’s going on.”

Federal Communications Commission (FCC) head Brendan Carr, a Trump ally, also dismissed concerns about the ads and called them “normal course public service announcements that you see all the time.”

“There’s nothing in there that strikes me as out of the ordinary or that would merit any sort of FCC review,” Carr added. “There are groups on the left that have long worked and pushed to weaponize the FCC’s license renewal process. I’m sure they’ll do it again in the future. Again with respect to these, they are normal PSAs that don’t raise any red flags.”

Carr has launched investigations into several media companies with news and entertainment divisions that publish reporting and commentary critical of Trump.

Some Democrats have called on the U.S. Government Accountability Office to investigate the ads. A letter sent by Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and George Whitesides (D-Calif.) asked why tax money going to the federal government is paying for “desperate preelection propaganda.”

The letter accuses the ads of violating several laws, including the Consolidated Appropriations Act and the Antideficiency Act.

articles.title: Tillis says Trump impeachment over Jan 6 was ‘weighty,’ a ‘vote of no confidence’
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Monday said President Trump’s impeachment in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol Hill attack was “weighty” and his impeachment trial was a “vote of no confidence.” MS NOW’s Ari Melber spoke with Tillis on “The Beat,” where the two talked about Tillis’s upcoming book “How to Lose Friends and…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Monday said President Trump’s impeachment in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol Hill attack was “weighty” and his impeachment trial was a “vote of no confidence.”

MS NOW’s Ari Melber spoke with Tillis on “ The Beat ,” where the two talked about Tillis’s upcoming book “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” which comes out Tuesday. Melber played footage of Trump’s remarks to people charged and convicted of the attack, including Trump’s warning that “those who broke the law, you will pay.”

Melber then asked the senator if the Senate should hold the president accountable after he pardoned everyone charged and convicted.

“What trial was there?” Tillis asked. “I mean, there was no counsel. There were no witnesses. It was a vote of no confidence. If they had gone and spent the time that, historically, you spend with something as weighty as impeaching the President of the United States, maybe they could have convinced me. But it was a snap impeachment.”

Tillis said the premise of his memoir “is until both parties recognize that they are responsible for this escalation, beginning with Obama up to Trump 2, then you’re only going to find elections –– taking one party out of power, putting another one in and they will justify their abhorrent behavior based upon the behavior of the prior administration and so on and so forth.”

Melber returned to his question, to which Tillis replied that as long as the precedent is in place for a fast impeachment trial, it will only be diminished further when used against a future president facing impeachable offenses.

Tillis voted to acquit Trump, and he defended his choice in a recent interview with Ross Douthat for CBS News’s “60 Minutes.”

“What you’re doing is a means-justifies-the-end rationalization,” the North Carolina Republican said about Trump’s quick second impeachment. “So cheapening the impeachment process to prevent someone from running in the future, I just don’t buy it.”

During the part of the conversation about the Jan. 6 attack, Tillis warned that Trump could lash out at Republicans if they lose Congress after the November midterm elections.

Tillis said it would be a mistake for Trump to attack GOP lawmakers if the party loses badly in November, pointing to his low approval rating and voters’ concerns over affordability.

“It would be another political unforced error if we do that,” Tillis told Douthat.

Tillis, who parted with the president over the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act, announced last year that he would not seek reelection this November. Trump lashed out, calling him a “talker and complainer, NOT A DOER.”

articles.title: Gabriel Rufián se irá "a su casa" si ERC no respeta un "mínimo de condiciones"
articles.standfirst: El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso estudia su papel en las elecciones del 29 de noviembre
articles.summary: El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso estudia su papel en las elecciones del 29 de noviembre
articles.body: El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso de los Diputados, Gabriel Rufián, estudia su papel de cara a las próximas elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. El catalán, según ha informado EFE citando a fuentes cercanas al político, espera que su partido respete "un mínimo de condiciones de trabajo e influencia en la línea estratégica" de cara a estos comicios. Si no se cumplen, "se irá a su casa". Gabriel Rufián, portavoz de ERC desde 2019, opina, según esas fuentes, que se ha "roto la cara" por su formación política y cree que tiene galones para marcar mínimamente la línea del partido. Recordemos que el de Santa Coloma es partidario de una confluencia de las izquierdas de cara a estas elecciones generales. Esa postura, según insiste EFE, no es muy bien recibida por los dirigentes del grupo independentista. "Yo quiero someter al Estado y al PSOE, lo venimos haciendo los últimos seis años. Si Sumar, Podemos y la madre que nos parió no nos ponemos de acuerdo, nos merecemos que nos arrasen", afirmó Gabriel Rufián en declaraciones a 'Salvados', en La Sexta, el domingo, antes de la convocatoria oficial de elecciones generales. "La mejor opción es la de confluencia provincia por provincia. Está (Rufián) escuchando a todo el mundo porque todo el mundo le está llamando", ha asegurado a EFE una persona cerca a Rufián. Pese a todo, voces autorizadas de ERC consideran a Gabriel Rufián un enorme activo de cara a las próximas elecciones generales, el próximo 29 de noviembre. La secretaria general de ERC, Elisenda Alamany, ha destacado la figura de su actual portavoz en el Congreso de los Diputados, donde actualmente su formación tiene siete escaños. "Rufián es el mejor valor electoral que tiene nuestro partido para esta convocatoria, pero hay un proceso que se debe cumplir", ha indicado en una rueda de prensa.
